subject: Fluid Mechanics
summary: streamlines, stream function and velocity potential, continuity and control-volume mass balance, acceleration of fluid particles, vorticity and circulation, basic potential flows, and Bernoulli's equation

questions.text: The streamlines of the two-dimensional flow u = x, v = −y are
solution: Concept: A streamline is everywhere tangent to the velocity: dx/u = dy/v.
dx/x = dy/(−y) → ln x = −ln y + c → xy = constant (rectangular hyperbolas, with a stagnation point at the origin; see the sketch).
Exam tip: This is the flow towards a flat wall (stagnation-point flow). Its ψ is xy, and its φ is (x² − y²)/2.

questions.text: For a three-dimensional incompressible flow, u = 3x² and v = −2xy, and w = 0 on the plane z = 0. The value of w at the point (1, 1, 2) is ______
solution: Concept: Continuity for incompressible flow: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0.
∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 6x − 2x = 4x, so ∂w/∂z = −4x and w = −4xz + f(x, y).
w = 0 at z = 0 gives f = 0, so w = −4xz = −4 × 1 × 2 = -8
Exam tip: When integrating with respect to z, the 'constant' can be a function of x and y; use the boundary condition to fix it.

questions.text: The stream function of a two-dimensional flow is ψ = 3xy (SI units). The speed at the point (2, 1) (in m/s, round off to two decimal places) is ______ (Take u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x and u = ∂φ/∂x, v = ∂φ/∂y.)
solution: Concept: Velocity components from the stream function: u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x.
Exam tip: Check the sign convention in the question; some books use u = −∂ψ/∂y. The speed comes out the same either way.

questions.text: A velocity potential φ exists for a flow only if the flow is
solution: Concept: If V = ∇φ, then curl V = curl(∇φ) = 0 identically. So φ can exist only where the vorticity is zero.
Compressibility, steadiness or dimension do not matter; the flow must be irrotational.
Exam tip: ψ needs continuity (2-D); φ needs irrotationality. Both exist together only for 2-D, incompressible, irrotational (potential) flow, and then both satisfy Laplace's equation.

questions.text: The velocity potential of a two-dimensional flow is φ = 3xy (SI units). If the stream function is zero at the origin, its value at the point (1, 3) is ______ (Take u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x and u = ∂φ/∂x, v = ∂φ/∂y.)
solution: Concept: Use u = ∂φ/∂x = ∂ψ/∂y and v = ∂φ/∂y = −∂ψ/∂x (Cauchy–Riemann relations).
Exam tip: Lines of constant φ (hyperbolas xy = c) and constant ψ (hyperbolas y² − x² = c) cross at right angles: a flow net.

questions.text: A two-dimensional unsteady flow has u = 2xt and v = −2yt (SI units). The magnitude of the acceleration of a fluid particle at the point (1, 2) at t = 1 s (in m/s², round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Total acceleration = local (∂V/∂t) + convective (u ∂V/∂x + v ∂V/∂y).
Exam tip: Don't drop the local term: in unsteady flow ∂u/∂t is non-zero even at a fixed point.

questions.text: Which statement about a flow net is NOT correct?
opts: Streamlines and equipotential lines intersect at right angles
The discharge between any two adjacent streamlines is the same
Where streamlines crowd together the velocity is high
A flow net can be drawn for rotational flows near solid boundaries
questions.ans: (D) A flow net can be drawn for rotational flows near solid boundaries
solution: Concept: A flow net is the grid of streamlines (ψ = const) and equipotential lines (φ = const). It needs φ, so the flow must be irrotational (potential flow).
(A), (B) and (C) are true: the two families are orthogonal, the discharge between adjacent streamlines is constant, and closer streamlines mean higher velocity.
(D) is false: near walls viscous effects make the flow rotational (boundary layer), where no φ and hence no flow net exists. Answer (D)
Exam tip: Flow nets are used for seepage under dams and for flow outside the boundary layer.

questions.text: For the velocity field u = −3y, v = 3x (SI units), the circulation around a circle of radius 0.5 m centred at the origin (in m²/s, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Stokes' theorem: circulation Γ = ∮V·dr = ∬ωz dA, with vorticity ωz = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y.
ωz = 3 − (−3) = 6 s⁻¹ (uniform: a forced vortex rotating at 3 rad/s)
Check directly: on r = 0.5 the speed is 3r = 1.5 m/s, so Γ = 1.5 × 2π(0.5) = 4.71 m²/s.
Exam tip: Angular velocity = vorticity/2 = 3 rad/s.

questions.text: Water flows at 0.08 m³/s through the horizontal pipe shown, which tapers from 250 mm diameter at section 1 to 125 mm at section 2. The gauge pressure at section 1 is 150 kPa. Neglecting losses, the gauge pressure at section 2 (in kPa, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Continuity gives the velocities; Bernoulli (z1 = z2) then gives the pressure drop.
Exam tip: Halving the diameter makes V four times larger and the kinetic head sixteen times larger.

questions.text: At a point in a pipeline carrying water, the velocity is 4 m/s, the gauge pressure is 40 kPa and the elevation above the datum is 6 m. The total energy head at the point (in m of water, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Total head H = p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z (pressure head + velocity head + datum head).
Exam tip: The hydraulic grade line is p/ρg + z (here 10.08 m); the energy line is a velocity head above it.

questions.text: A water jet issues from a nozzle at 20 m/s, inclined at 60° to the horizontal. Neglecting air resistance, the maximum height reached by the jet above the nozzle is
solution: Concept: In a free jet the pressure is atmospheric throughout and the horizontal velocity component stays constant. At the top only V cos θ remains.
Bernoulli between the nozzle and the top: V²/2g = (V cos θ)²/2g + h → h = V² sin²θ/(2g)
Exam tip: 20.39 m is the height for a vertical jet (θ = 90°); 5.10 m uses cos²θ by mistake.

questions.text: Air leaks from a rigid tank of volume 0.5 m³ through a small hole of area 50 mm². At an instant the air in the hole has a density of 6 kg/m³ and a velocity of 200 m/s. The rate of change of the density of the air in the tank at that instant (in kg/m³ per s, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Unsteady control-volume mass balance: d(ρVtank)/dt + ṁout = 0.
dρ/dt = −ṁout/Vtank = −0.06/0.5 = -0.12 kg/m³ per s (density falling)
Exam tip: The sign matters in NAT: a decreasing density gives a negative answer.

questions.text: The flow past a long circular cylinder (without circulation) can be obtained by superposing a uniform flow on a
solution: Concept: A doublet is a source and sink of equal strength brought together. Added to a uniform flow U, the streamline ψ = 0 becomes a circle of radius a = √(μ/2πU).
Uniform flow + source → Rankine half-body; uniform flow + source + sink (separated) → Rankine oval; uniform flow + doublet → circular cylinder; adding a free vortex gives lift (Magnus effect).
Exam tip: On the cylinder surface the speed is 2U sin θ: maximum 2U at the top and bottom, zero at the two stagnation points.

questions.text: A closed tank contains water with air at 50 kPa (gauge) above it. Water discharges to the atmosphere through a small nozzle 2 m below the water surface, as shown. Neglecting losses, the velocity of the jet (in m/s, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Bernoulli from the water surface (V ≈ 0, p = 50 kPa gauge) to the jet (p = 0 gauge): V = √[2(p/ρ + gh)].
The air pressure is equivalent to an extra head of 50000/9810 = 5.10 m of water, so the effective head is 7.10 m.
Exam tip: Ignoring the air pressure gives √(2g × 2) = 6.26 m/s, a common slip.

questions.text: Which statement about a free (irrotational) vortex is correct?
opts: The tangential velocity varies inversely with the radius, and Bernoulli's constant is the same for all streamlines
The tangential velocity is proportional to the radius, and the free surface is a paraboloid
The vorticity is uniform and equal to twice the angular velocity
The pressure decreases with increasing radius
questions.ans: (A) The tangential velocity varies inversely with the radius, and Bernoulli's constant is the same for all streamlines
solution: Concept: Free vortex: no external torque, so angular momentum is conserved: V r = constant (V ∝ 1/r). The flow is irrotational everywhere except at the centre.
Because it is irrotational, p/ρ + V²/2 + gz is the same constant on every streamline. In a forced vortex (V = ωr) the flow is rotational and the constant changes from one streamline to another.
Exam tip: Examples: free vortex — water draining from a basin, flow in a whirlpool chamber; forced vortex — a liquid rotating with its container (paraboloid surface).
